title: An agent that runs the paperwork for a rental house
summary: In one sitting, an AI agent turned a landlord's scattered to-do list into a working system: a shared folder, a capital plan that reflows itself, calendar deadlines and a handoff to my other agents. A written rulebook decides what it may touch.

stat.label: come first: a written rulebook sets what the agent does alone, what needs my word and what it never does

sections.heading: Problem
paragraphs: My household owns a rental house that we manage from out of state, with no property manager. The house is old enough that its original systems are reaching the end of their lives. The roof is the big one, the water heater is close behind, and a pile of smaller jobs trails after them: a microwave upgrade, a yearly backflow test and an air filter that needs changing on a schedule.

None of it lived in one place. A lease was changing, the insurance had to change with it, and every repair sat in my head as a vague worry instead of a plan. The real question was simple to ask and hard to answer: can the rent alone pay for all of it, and in what order should the work happen?

sections.heading: What I built
paragraphs: I gave an agent a job description. It runs as a named role, defined by a one-page brief in a Claude Project, and the brief is a rulebook with three columns. The first lists what the agent may do on its own: edit the lease document and read every change back, track dates on the shared finance calendar, keep the repair log and the capital plan, and read the listing site to draft text for me to post. The second lists what needs my word first: changing anything on the listing site, sharing a property file, sending updates to my other agents. The third lists what it never does: contact the tenant, sign anything, move money, waive a fee, or approve a change to the lease terms.

Inside those lines it built three tools around one folder that my own account owns. The folder holds the lease template, the signed leases, the receipts and a capital plan spreadsheet with four tabs for the reserve, the projects, the recurring chores and a log. The calendar holds the deadlines, from the insurance switch to the yearly backflow test. Email carries the handoff to my other agents, in a fixed format with a tagged subject, a header and a signature, and it only goes out when I ask. The agent can read the listing site through my browser and cannot change it.

The plan treats all the rent as a savings stream and pays for projects in priority order. Every target date in the sheet is a formula over the income, the balance and the running cost of the queue, so no date is typed in by hand.

sections.heading: Result
paragraphs: The answer was yes: rent alone pays for every project, the roof last. Because the dates are formulas, the plan never goes stale. A new quote, a bigger estimate or a missed month moves the whole schedule on its own, and nobody retypes a thing.

The session worked like a conversation, and the plan changed in the same breath as each decision. I corrected a filter size, a test date and a cost, and the agent updated the inputs and added yearly reminders. When I gave it the roof estimate, it pointed out that my target date for the roof landed before the money would exist, then tied that date to the funding date so it could never drift ahead of reality. When I asked whether my insurer could help with the water heater, it researched the coverage, found that wear and tear is excluded, and I decided to move to a rental policy first. It put that deadline on the calendar before the conversation moved on.

Two prompts mattered most. When I asked what I might be overlooking, the agent came back with a list of ten gaps across the lease, the money and the upkeep, and I cleared most of them on the spot. When I wondered whether my water heater budget was too thin, it checked local prices, told me the range was wider than I had assumed and recommended a bigger number. It also found licensed local plumbers I could call for quotes. I took the recommendation, and the plan rebuilt itself around it.

sections.heading: What went wrong
paragraphs: The agent got a prediction wrong, and said so. It told me a budget change would push the roof back a month, then recalculated and reported that the roof stayed where it was. I would rather have an agent that corrects itself in the open than one that quietly smooths over its misses.

Two conflicts surfaced and it left both to me instead of resolving them: the roof date against the money, and the choice of insurance policy. The numbers are also only as good as the estimates behind them. Until real quotes arrive, the plan is a well-organised guess. It assumes the rent arrives every month, so a vacancy would shift the whole schedule. And recurring reminders only fire once their last-done dates are filled in, so the air filter waits on a date from me.

sections.heading: Lesson
paragraphs: A short written rulebook beats trust. Because the agent knew in advance which actions were free, which needed my word and which were off the table, it moved fast on routine work and stopped at money, signatures and anything addressed to the tenant. The rulebook also gave me something to check each change against when I read it back.

Two other habits made the difference. Formulas beat typed numbers, since one new quote reflows the whole plan. And research is worth doing only if it ends in a decision: every lookup, from insurance coverage to repair prices to local plumbers, finished as a choice or a number I could act on. What is left is the human part: collecting a few quotes, filling in the filter date, switching the policy and filing the signed lease.

sources: Claude Docs artifact 'Case Study: Agentic Property Management for a Single-Family Rental', 2026-11-05 (the agent's one-session summary). Dollar figures, dates, location and vendor details removed for privacy
